messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

He is seventy-eight now, a divorced North American man who still introduces himself by his job title when people ask what he does. "Database administrator," he says, even though he has technically scaled back. The phrase seems to steady him. He likes systems, backups, clean structures, the comfort of knowing where things are stored and how they can be retrieved. Before he becomes ill, his life is organized in that same way. He lives alone, keeps regular hours, checks on servers remotely in the early morning, answers tickets, and takes a certain quiet pride in being the person who can restore order when something crashes.

The illness begins in a way that does not seem dramatic at first. He notices fatigue that does not fit, then shortness of breath walking from his car to the office. He tells himself he is getting older, that everyone slows down. He delays calling the doctor, annoyed by his own body for becoming unreliable. When he finally goes in, things move too quickly. There are tests, more tests, a specialist whose face changes as he reads the chart. He remembers fragments: the fluorescent lights, a nurse speaking too loudly, the cold vinyl of the exam table under his palms. What he understands clearly is that something inside him has gone badly wrong and could kill him.

The worst part comes during a hospitalization several weeks later, when his condition deteriorates suddenly. He cannot get enough air. He remembers the animal panic of trying to breathe and not being able to, the sensation that the room narrows to a single task his body is failing to perform. People rush in. Someone tells him to stay calm, which feels absurd. He sees a monitor alarm, hears shoes squeaking, catches words like "critical" and "unstable." At one point he is certain he is dying. He thinks, with surprising clarity, that his apartment is a mess, that no one knows the passwords to his systems, that he will vanish in a room full of strangers with tubes in his arms. The helplessness humiliates him as much as it terrifies him.

He survives, but he says the fear does not stay in the hospital. It follows him home and settles into his routines. In the first months after discharge, he sleeps in short stretches, waking abruptly with his chest tight and his heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that he is back in that room. He keeps a pulse oximeter on the bedside table and checks it repeatedly through the night. If he feels a little winded climbing stairs, his mind jumps immediately to catastrophe. He tells himself to be rational, but rational thought gives way to a flood of images: the monitor, the mask on his face, the feeling of air not coming.

During the day he becomes watchful in a way he never was before. He tracks bodily sensations the way he once tracked server performance, constantly scanning for signs of failure. A cough, a skipped heartbeat, a wave of fatigue-each one demands attention. He opens patient portals and rereads old test results as if he might catch something everyone else missed. He searches survival statistics online late into the night and then feels sick with dread after reading them. He avoids follow-up appointments for weeks at a time because he cannot bear the anticipatory fear, then becomes frantic that avoidance itself will cost him his life.

His work changes too. He still logs in to monitor databases, but his concentration is thinner. He used to enjoy solving complex problems; now, when an alert goes off, his body reacts as if it is another emergency room alarm. He startles at phone notifications. On bad days he stares at lines of code and realizes he has been rereading the same query without understanding it. He is embarrassed by mistakes that would once have been unthinkable. He tells coworkers he is "a little foggy," making a joke of it, but privately he worries that the illness has permanently damaged him.

Because he lives alone, there is no one to witness how much of his day is organized around not feeling vulnerable. He keeps medications lined up with mechanical precision. He sits near exits in waiting rooms. He avoids long drives, crowded places, and anywhere he imagines help would be slow to reach him if his body failed again. He has stopped going to a weekly breakfast he used to attend with former colleagues because one of them asked an innocent question about the hospital and he felt himself go cold all over, as if the memory were happening in the present.

When he talks about the illness now, he does so matter-of-factly at first, almost like documenting a system outage. But then his voice catches on details he cannot file away: the terror of not being able to breathe, the certainty that he was about to die, the shame of needing strangers to keep him alive. He says he used to think surviving would mean being done with it. Instead, he feels as though part of him is still in that hospital bed, braced for the next alarm, waiting for his body to betray him again.
